title: Feedback
intro: Feedback is the engine of analog precision: it turns a high-gain but poorly controlled amplifier into a lower-gain one whose behaviour is fixed by a few passive components. This chapter covers what feedback buys, the four ways to wire it, how to analyse real circuits where the loop cannot be cleanly separated, and the general methods of Bode, Blackman and Middlebrook (Razavi, Chapter 8).

blocks.alt: Block diagram of a negative-feedback system. The input x enters a summing node, where the feedback signal is subtracted. The difference e goes into the amplifier A, whose output is y. The output is fed back through the block beta to the summing node.
blocks.caption: The standard negative-feedback loop: a forward amplifier $A$ and a feedback network $\beta$.

blocks.text: A forward amplifier $H(s)$ amplifies the error between the input and a sensed copy of the output, $G(s)Y(s)$. Solving $Y = H(X - GY)$ gives the closed-loop transfer function. In most circuits here the feedback network is a frequency-independent fraction $\beta$ (a resistor or capacitor divider), so

blocks.caption: Closed-loop gain; the approximation holds for $\beta A \gg 1$.

blocks.text: The product $\beta A$ is the loop gain. Every benefit of feedback scales with $1 + \beta A$: gain sensitivity, bandwidth, terminal impedances and distortion all improve by this factor. Because the error is driven toward zero, the amplifier input is a virtual ground and the feedback signal becomes an accurate replica of the input.

Any feedback circuit contains four parts, even when they are hidden inside a single transistor: the forward amplifier, a way of sensing the output (voltage or current), the feedback network, and a way of comparing (subtracting) at the input. A source-degenerated common-source stage is a feedback circuit: $R_S$ senses the drain current and subtracts the resulting voltage from the gate drive.

Set the main input to zero, break the loop, inject a test signal $V_t$ in the forward direction, follow it round and find the returned signal $V_F$. The loop gain is $-V_F/V_t$. It is dimensionless, and it does not depend on where the input and output are taken, so circuits that look different (for example a feedback common-source and a feedback common-gate stage built from the same parts) can have the same loop gain. Where to break the loop without disturbing loading is the subject of the loading and Bode pages.

items: Properties of Feedback: gain desensitization, impedance modification, bandwidth extension, linearity, noise, and the four amplifier types.
Feedback Topologies: voltage-voltage, current-voltage, voltage-current and current-current feedback with circuit examples, and how sensing and returning set $R_{in}$ and $R_{out}$.
Loading and Two-Port Analysis: why breaking the loop is hard, the five classic difficulties, and the two-port recipe that includes the feedback network's loading.

Bode, Blackman and Loop-Gain Methods: return ratio, Bode's A-B-C-D formulation, Blackman's impedance theorem, the asymptotic-gain and double-null forms, Middlebrook's method, and where to break a loop.

blocks.text: Feedback does not come free: it lowers the gain by $1 + \beta A$, the feedback network loads the amplifier, and a loop with too much phase shift oscillates. Stability is Chapter 10.

blocks.title: Loop gain from accuracy
blocks.text: A closed-loop amplifier must have a gain of 8 with an error below 0.5%. What is the minimum open-loop gain $A$?
solution: The relative error is about $1/(\beta A)$, so $\beta A \ge 200$.
